issues.legal_issue: Subordinate legislation must be published or promulgated in a suitable manner before it takes effect, and a publication method prescribed by the parent law must be followed.
material_facts: The dispute concerned whether an approved planning scheme had become effective despite the form in which it was published.
The governing law prescribed a publication method for the approved plan and its regulations.
issues.conclusion: Subordinate legislation must be made known through suitable publication or promulgation to take effect; where the parent law prescribes the method, that method must be followed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that subordinate legislation must be published or promulgated in a suitable manner whether or not the parent law expressly requires publication. If the parent law prescribes the method, that method governs; if it is silent, a reasonable method prescribed by the subordinate legislation may suffice, otherwise publication through the Official Gazette or another reasonable method is required. The Court referred to Narayana Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh on publication by a suitable method.

rule.if: subordinate_legislation_effectiveness_dispute and ((parent_law_specifies_publication_mode and prescribed_publication_mode_followed) or (not parent_law_specifies_publication_mode and ((subordinate_rule_specifies_reasonable_mode and subordinate_rule_mode_followed) or (not subordinate_rule_specifies_reasonable_mode and suitable_publication_used))))

predicates.subordinate_legislation_effectiveness_di: The proceeding challenges whether a rule or other subordinate law has taken effect.
predicates.parent_law_specifies_publication_mode: The law authorising the subordinate legislation specifies how it must be published or promulgated.
predicates.prescribed_publication_mode_followed: The subordinate legislation was published or promulgated using the method specified by the authorising law.
predicates.subordinate_rule_specifies_reasonable_mo: The subordinate legislation itself specifies a reasonable method of publication or promulgation.
predicates.subordinate_rule_mode_followed: The subordinate legislation was published or promulgated using the reasonable method it specifies.
predicates.suitable_publication_used: The subordinate legislation was published through a customary official channel or another suitable method.

issues.definition: Subordinate legislation is effective when the applicable prescribed publication method is followed or, where no method is prescribed, a suitable publication method is used.

issues.legal_issue: A Gazette notice informing the public that an approved planning plan and its regulations are available for inspection can satisfy the requirement to publish them.
material_facts: Gazette notices at successive stages informed the public that the planning plan was available for inspection at the planning authority’s office.
The plan and its regulations were kept available for inspection, and the authorities treated the plan as including the regulations.
A notice concerning the provisionally approved plan invited public comments, and about 600 representations and objections were received.
The final Gazette notice stated that the approved plan and report were available for inspection, although the plan and regulations were not reproduced in full in the Gazette.
issues.conclusion: The notices and inspection arrangements complied with the statutory and regulatory publication requirements; the plan and regulations did not have to be reproduced in full in the Gazette.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 9 and 13(1) and (4) of the Mysore Town and Country Planning Act, 1961, and Rules 32 and 33 of the Mysore Planning Authority Rules, 1965, read together, required Gazette notice of the plan’s availability for inspection, permanent display, and public access to a copy. Rule 33 did not require the plan and regulations to be bodily incorporated in the Gazette. The Court distinguished Shalagram Jhajharia v. National Co. Ltd. and Firestone Tyre & Rubber Co. v. Synthetics & Chemicals Ltd., which concerned disclosure requirements for company meetings, and Municipal Board, Pushkar v. State Transport Authority and Joint Chief Controller of Imports & Exports v. Aminchand Mutha, which concerned different publication issues. It also applied the principle that an interpretation departing from the common understanding of the statutory scheme should not be adopted without justification.

predicates.planning_scheme_publication_dispute: The proceeding challenges whether an approved planning scheme was adequately published.
predicates.gazette_notice_announced_inspection: A notice in the official gazette told the public that the planning material could be inspected.
predicates.plan_and_regulations_available_for_inspe: The plan and its implementing regulations were available for public inspection at the relevant authority’s office.

issues.definition: When a publication dispute concerns a planning scheme, a Gazette notice announcing inspection satisfies the publication requirement if the plan and its regulations are available for inspection.

issues.legal_issue: A publication defect that has otherwise served its purpose and caused no substantial injustice may be cured by a statutory validation provision.
material_facts: The authority attempted to bring the plan and regulations to public attention through Gazette notices and inspection arrangements.
The appellants did not initially plead that the plan had not been published or that they lacked knowledge of its requirements; they instead claimed to have complied with them.
The Court found that the defect or irregularity had not affected the merits of the case.
issues.conclusion: Any defect in publication was curable under the statutory validation provision because the publication attempt had served its purpose and the defect caused no substantial injustice.
issues.legal_principle: Section 76J of the Mysore Town and Country Planning Act, 1961, validated acts and proceedings affected by specified defects or irregularities not affecting the merits of the case. The Court relied on Bangalore Woollen, Cotton & Silk Mills Co. Ltd. v. Corporation of the City of Bangalore and Municipal Board, Sitapur v. Prayag Narain Saigal, which treated non-publication defects as curable where they had not affected the merits or caused substantial prejudice. The Court also observed that the mandatory-or-directory distinction is determined by the statutory object and context, not by a simple formula, referring to Liverpool Borough v. Turner.

rule.if: planning_scheme_publication_challenge and publication_defect and public_notice_attempted and defect_caused_no_substantial_injustice

predicates.planning_scheme_publication_challenge: The proceeding challenges the effectiveness of a planning scheme because of an alleged publication defect.
predicates.publication_defect: A required publication step was defective or incomplete.
predicates.public_notice_attempted: The responsible authority made an effort to bring the planning scheme to the public’s attention.
predicates.defect_caused_no_substantial_injustice: The publication defect did not affect the merits or cause substantial injustice.

issues.definition: A publication defect in a challenged planning scheme is cured when the authority attempted public notice and the defect caused no substantial injustice.

issues.legal_issue: Regulations that implement and give effect to a planning plan form part of the plan rather than constituting a separate instrument for publication purposes.
material_facts: The regulations governed land use and gave practical effect to the planning plan.
The plan and regulations were treated by the authorities as a single planning scheme and were kept available together for inspection.
The final notice referred to the plan but did not separately mention the regulations.
issues.conclusion: The regulations were an integral part of the plan, and the notice’s failure to name them separately did not establish that they were unavailable for inspection or unpublished.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 12(2), 13 and 14 of the Mysore Town and Country Planning Act, 1961, the regulations were connected to the plan, supplied its operative detail, and helped enforce its provisions. The statutory references to the plan and the regulations identified different components for different procedural purposes; they did not make the regulations separate from the overall plan.

predicates.planning_scheme_components_dispute: The proceeding disputes whether regulations associated with a planning plan are separate from the plan.
predicates.regulations_implement_plan: The regulations provide the rules needed to make the plan effective.
predicates.plan_and_regulations_kept_together: The authority treated and maintained the plan and its regulations together for public access.

issues.definition: Regulations form part of a planning plan when they implement it and the authority maintains the two together.
